claim: ExecStopPost= in systemd.service(5) defines additional commands executed after the service is stopped, covering all exit paths: when ExecStop= was used, when no ExecStop= is defined, and when the service exited unexpectedly — making it the correct hook for post-mortem/failure cleanup, whereas ExecStop= is recommended for requesting clean termination.
stance_target: agent helper units and failure-notification hooks should use ExecStopPost= since it fires on failure paths (including failed startup), matching the KDE thread's recommendation with canonical semantics
scope_conditions: systemd service units; [Service] section; $MAINPID unset when main process already exited
quoted_support: ExecStopPost= Additional commands that are executed after the service is stopped. This includes cases where the commands configured in ExecStop= were used, where the service does not have any ExecStop= defined, or where the service exited unexpectedly. ... It is recommended to use this setting for commands that communicate with the service requesting clean termination. For post-mortem clean-up steps use ExecStopPost= instead.

claim: Service restarts are implemented as stop operations followed by start operations, so ExecStop= and ExecStopPost= both execute during every service restart — failure-hook logic in ExecStopPost must tolerate restarts and should distinguish failure exit codes.
stance_target: agent notification hooks must not fire user-visible alerts on routine restarts — they need exit-status awareness
quoted_support: Service restart requests are implemented as stop operations followed by start operations. This means that ExecStop= and ExecStopPost= are executed during a service restart operation.

claim: systemd supports service templates (service@argument.service, instantiated from a template unit) and systemd-run can create transient .service and .scope units dynamically from the command line — the mechanism for agent-initiated, on-the-fly units without writing unit files.
stance_target: the agent can run fleet operations as transient scoped units (systemd-run --unit=...) so its actions are visible/supervisable in systemd, rather than detached child processes
quoted_support: The systemd-run command allows creating .service and .scope units dynamically and transiently from the command line. ... It is possible for systemd services to take a single argument via the service@argument.service syntax. Such services are called "instantiated" services
